title: The Jewish calendar
hookLine: a lunar year with a leap month seven times in nineteen years, so festivals keep their seasons

cards: Ask a Jewish friend when Hanukkah is this year, and there's a good chance they'll have to look it up. One year it starts in late November. Another year it lands right on top of Christmas.
Passover drifts around March and April. Rosh Hashanah can come in early September or in October. It looks like the holidays wander.
They don't. They're keeping time, just not by the clock on your phone. For the next few weeks, i'll walk you through the Jewish year, one holiday at a time, as they arrive.
First, the thing that holds them all.

teach.b: The Hebrew word for a calendar is luach: a tablet or a board, the same word used for the tablets Moses carried down the mountain. Today a luach is often a printed calendar on a synagogue wall, or an app.
The Jewish calendar runs on the moon.

teach.h: EACH MONTH BEGINS AT THE NEW MOON.
teach.b: Each month begins at the new moon and lasts twenty-nine or thirty days, the time the moon takes to go from dark to dark.

In the first chapter of Genesis, the lights in the sky are made "for signs, and for seasons, and for days and years." The Psalms say it plainly: "Who appointedst the moon for seasons." Here's the problem.
Twelve moon months fall about eleven days short of the sun's year. A purely lunar calendar slides backward through the seasons, and the Torah ties Passover to spring and Sukkot to the harvest.

teach.h: A LEAP MONTH, SEVEN TIMES IN NINETEEN.
teach.b: So, seven times in every nineteen years, the calendar adds a whole extra month, a second Adar, in late winter. That pulls the moon back in line with the sun, and Passover stays in spring.
For centuries, a court in Jerusalem declared each new month when witnesses reported seeing the thin new moon.
Later, tradition says in the fourth century, the calendar was fixed by calculation, so Jews scattered around the world could keep the same days.
A Jewish day begins at sunset, because Genesis says "there was evening and there was morning."
And the years are counted from creation, as the rabbis reckoned it, which is why a Hebrew year number runs into the five thousands.

how: Jewish communities keep a lunisolar calendar: months follow the moon, a second Adar is added seven times in nineteen years, and each day, Shabbat and festival begins at sunset. Many families keep a printed luach from their synagogue.

games.q: what's inside the calendar — tap the pairs.

s: the Jewish holidays move around from year to year
they stay on the same Hebrew date. it's the sun's calendar that makes them look like they wander.
a purely lunar year is about eleven days short of the sun's
that's why the calendar adds a leap month seven times in nineteen years.
new months were once declared by witnesses who saw the moon

games.q: you're keeping a calendar of moon months, and Passover must stay in spring. after a few years it's drifting toward winter. what do you do?
o: drop the moon and count by the sun alone.
add a whole extra month every few years.
let Passover drift through the seasons.
games.why: the Jewish calendar adds a second Adar seven times in nineteen years, so the moon keeps the months and the festivals keep their seasons.

practice: Notice the time of day you're in; if it's evening, on this calendar tomorrow has already begun. Think of one date that matters to you, a birthday, an anniversary, the day someone died, and wonder what it was on the moon's calendar.
Just hold the idea that there's more than one way to count a life.

wordCard.voice: Luach. A tablet, and the Jewish calendar: moon months, kept in step with the sun by a leap month seven times in nineteen years.
